families.s: HSE COSHH control of cleaning substances
families.t: risk assessment, prevention or control, storage, handling, disposal, spills, corrosives, vapours, mists, PPE and training
f: COSHH requires assessment of risks from cleaning substances.
The assessment should include storage, handling, disposal, accidents and serious spillages.
Exposure should be prevented or adequately controlled.
Cleaning products may be corrosive and can cause burns or eye damage.
Some ingredients can cause skin allergy or asthma.
Work techniques should minimise leaks, splashes, sprays and spills.
Protective gloves, aprons and eye protection may be needed for residual risk.
Workers need information, instruction and training on hazards, dilution, PPE and emergency action.
families.g: Cleaning COSHH risk depends on chemical and concentration, task and form, storage and dilution, spray and splash, ventilation, PPE, worker susceptibility, spill response and training.

families.t: mopping, wiping, polishing, rubbish, furniture, machines, repetition, force, posture, pushing and pulling, equipment design and maintenance
f: Musculoskeletal disorders are the most commonly reported work-related ill health or injury among cleaners.
Cleaning is labour intensive and often involves repetitive or forceful work.
Mopping, wiping and polishing can strain the back, neck, shoulders and upper limbs.
Moving rubbish bags, furniture and equipment can create heavy manual-handling demands.
Assessment should cover lifting, carrying, pushing, pulling, reaching and operating controls.
Restricted workspaces and poor equipment design can increase awkward posture and force.
Heavy or poorly maintained machines can increase physical effort.
Task design, equipment selection, maintenance, work organisation and recovery time should be considered together.
families.g: Cleaning MSD risk depends on task frequency and force, posture and reach, load and equipment, floor and workspace, machine condition, pace, staffing, individual capability and recovery.

families.s: HSE cleaning task, equipment and work-design risk-control guidance
families.t: all tasks, individual capacity, loads, environment, time pressure, restricted space, equipment availability, forceful movement, maintenance and supervision
f: Cleaning risk assessment should consider all tasks performed rather than only routine floor cleaning.
The individual capacity of the cleaner should be considered.
Loads, equipment and the work environment are core assessment factors.
Time pressure can encourage unsafe pace or methods.
Restricted space can increase awkward movement and handling risk.
Lack of suitable equipment can force excessive manual effort.
Poorly maintained equipment can increase force and loss-of-control risk.
Work methods, training and supervision should match the selected equipment and actual premises.
families.g: Cleaning work-design risk depends on task range, worker capability, equipment and maintenance, available space and time, load, floor and access, staffing, instruction and supervision.

families.s: HSE work-at-height control for cleaning activities
families.t: avoidance, planning, supervision, competence, equipment selection, inspection, fragile surfaces, access, fall prevention and rescue
f: Cleaning work at height should be avoided where reasonably practicable.
Where it cannot be avoided, it should be properly planned and supervised.
People carrying out the work should be competent for the method and equipment.
The right access equipment should be selected for the height, duration and task.
Equipment exposed to deterioration should be inspected at suitable intervals.
The assessment should consider people below and prevent falling objects or contamination.
Fall prevention should take priority over relying only on personal fall-arrest equipment.
Emergency and rescue arrangements should be planned before the work begins.
families.g: Cleaning work-at-height risk depends on height and duration, surface and edge, access method and equipment, weather, people below, inspection, competence, supervision and rescue.

families.s: HSE window-cleaning work-at-height planning and rescue guidance
families.t: water-fed poles, internal cleaning, ladders, MEWPs, ropes, anchor points, PPE, inspection, cooperation and rescue
f: Window-cleaning work should avoid height where practicable, for example by using water-fed poles or cleaning from inside.
Work at height must be planned, supervised and carried out by competent people.
Equipment should be selected for the building, access, height and duration.
Equipment liable to deteriorate should be inspected regularly and after exceptional events.
Fall-arrest anchor points require periodic inspection and testing by a competent person.
Appropriate PPE and training are required where residual risks remain.
Rescue procedures must be planned before work starts and cannot rely only on emergency services.
Property owners, managing agents, contractors and workers should cooperate and communicate about access and rescue.
families.g: Window-cleaning risk depends on building and glazing, access method and height, weather and surface, equipment and anchors, people below, inspection, competence, cooperation and rescue.
